Lorenzo Ghiberti. The Florentine sculptor and goldsmith whose bronze doors for the Florence Baptistry became a defining monument of the early Renaissance. His narrative reliefs—depicting biblical scenes with architectural depth and naturalistic figures—influenced an entire generation and proved sculpture's capacity for complex storytelling.

Ghiberti designed and cast the North Doors from 1403 to 1424 of the Florence Baptistry, depicting New Testament scenes with elegant Gothic-Renaissance hybrid style. He created the celebrated East Doors from 1425 to 1452, later called the Gates of Paradise, with ten Old Testament scenes framed in mathematical perspective. Ghiberti pioneered linear perspective in relief sculpture, creating architectural landscapes and vistas within shallow bronze fields. He mastered intricate narrative relief, layering multiple figures and temporal moments within unified compositions.

Ghiberti worked as both sculptor and goldsmith, bringing jeweler's precision and decorative sophistication to large-scale bronzes. He won the famous 1401 competition for the Baptistry doors, establishing his reputation and launching the Florentine Renaissance. His two monumental Baptistry door commissions defined Renaissance architectural sculpture and stand at the heart of Florence's cathedral complex. Though his contemporary Donatello favored more austere narrative, Ghiberti's more ornate approach proved foundational to the Florentine Renaissance style.
